line: Every word in a sentence has a job. The word class is the name of the job, not the name of the word.
The same word can do different jobs. 'He folds the letter' — verb. 'The letter had folds' — noun.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — what is it doing here?
line: Ask what the word is doing in this sentence, not what it usually is. This is the trick the test uses most: a word you know as one class doing another job.
castle and hill name things. stood is what happened. If you can put 'the' in front of it, it is probably a noun.
crumbling describes the castle. An adverb would describe the standing. Adjectives describe things, adverbs describe actions. That is the difference in one line.

section: step 4 — the tall tree with silver leaves
line: A noun phrase is the noun plus the words that tell you more about it. Find the noun first: tree.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.

line: That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“The goat ate the grass.” Who did the eating?
The one doing the verb is the subject. The one it’s done to is the object.
Here is how to do it.
Start with the verb, the action. Everything else is about who does it and to what.
The one doing it is the subject. The subject usually comes before the verb.
The one it’s done to is the object. The object usually comes after the verb.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Four kinds of sentence: statement, question, command, exclamation. Each has its own job and its own ending.
An exclamation must start with What or How and have a verb. 'What a brilliant song this is!' Not just anything with an exclamation mark.
Here is how to do it.
'We watched the game together.' Full stop. Most sentences are statements. Check the others first and this one is what is left.

section: step 2 — commands tell you to do something
line: 'Hold the handrail.' They usually start with the verb. A command has no visible subject — the 'you' is understood.

section: step 3 — exclamations are the strict one
line: They must begin What or How AND have a verb. 'What a mess!' is not an exclamation in this test — no verb. This is the marks people lose.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“It’s hot today, isn’t it?” The little question on the end is a question tag.
Question tags check that someone agrees.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — find the helping verb: are
line: You’re means you are. The tag repeats the helping verb.
Positive sentence, negative tag. A negative sentence gets a positive tag: It isn’t raining, is it?
Add the pronoun and a question mark. The tag always ends with a question mark.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“We ate under the mango tree because it was hot.”
Which part could stand on its own as a sentence?
Here is how to do it.
Read each part on its own. A main clause makes sense alone.

section: step 2 — “We ate under the mango tree” ✓
line: This works as a sentence. It has a subject and a verb and is complete.
This needs the rest. It starts with a subordinating conjunction, so it can’t stand alone.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“My uncle, who lives in Labé, keeps bees.”
The part between the commas tells you more about my uncle.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — find the noun: my uncle
line: What is the extra information about? A relative clause adds detail to a noun.
It starts with a relative pronoun. who for people, which for things, whose for belonging.
My uncle keeps bees. That shows it was extra information.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“a dog” tells you very little.
“a small brown dog with a red collar” paints a picture.
Here is how to do it.
Find the main noun. Everything else is built around it.
Adjectives come before the noun. They describe it.

section: step 3 — after: with a red collar
line: A prepositional phrase can follow it. It adds more detail.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“I wanted to play, but it was raining.”
Two main clauses, joined by one small word.
Here is how to do it.
Each half could be a sentence. Co-ordinating conjunctions join equals.
for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. These are the co-ordinating conjunctions.
Choose the one that fits the meaning. and adds, but contrasts, or gives a choice, so gives a result.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A clause is a piece of sentence with its own verb. Most sentences are built from two or more.
A main clause can stand alone. A subordinate clause cannot — it leans on the main one.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — cover half and read it
line: 'I walked to school' works alone. That is the main clause. This test works every time and needs nothing memorised.
'as we live on the same road' cannot stand alone. Subordinate. The joining word at the front — as, because, although, before — is what makes it lean.

section: step 3 — relative clauses describe a noun
line: 'who lives on a farm' tells you which uncle. It starts with who, which or that. A relative clause is a kind of subordinate clause, sitting next to the noun it describes.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“Yesterday Amina walked to the market.”
The time word tells you the tense before you read the verb.
Here is how to do it.
Look for when it happens. Yesterday, last week: past. Every day, always: present.
Most verbs add -ed in the past. Some are irregular: go → went, win → won.
Yesterday Amina walked to the market. Check the whole sentence sounds right.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“She has finished her homework.”
It happened in the past, but it matters now.
Here is how to do it.
Start with has (he, she, it) or have (I, you, we, they). That’s what makes it the present perfect.
Add the past participle. Irregular ones: seen, been, written, eaten.
She has finished her homework. The simple past would be: she finished.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Modal verbs are a dial for how certain something is. must, will, might, could, should.
They will walk home. They might walk home. One is a fact, the other is a maybe.
Here is how to do it.
It sits just before the main verb. must, shall, will, should, would, can, could, may, might — that is the whole list.
will and must are certain. might and could are possible. The test asks you to explain the difference in words, so practise saying it.
should is what ought to happen, not what will. Expectation, not certainty. That distinction has been asked before.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“While we were eating, the lights went out.”
The eating was going on when something else happened.
Here is how to do it.
Past progressive uses was or were. Present progressive uses am, is or are.
Add the -ing form. That shows it was going on.
While we were eating dinner… It shows an action in progress.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Tense tells the reader when something happened. Get it wrong halfway through and the sentence trips.
The test mostly checks consistency: if you start in the past, you finish in the past.
Here is how to do it.
Yesterday tells you this is the past before you read the verbs. There is almost always a clue like this. Find it first and the verbs follow.

section: step 2 — all the verbs must match
line: walked and opened, not walked and opens. One verb in the wrong tense loses the mark even if the rest are right.

section: step 3 — helpers change the tense too
line: was walking, had eaten — the helper is part of the verb. Progressive needs was or were. Perfect needs had or have. Learn those two pairs.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“If I were you, I would ask for help.”
You’re not me, so it isn’t real. That’s when the subjunctive is used.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — is it real or wished?
line: Wishes and ‘if’ situations that aren’t real. Also demands: She insisted that he be on time.
Even with I, he or she. In speech people say was, but the formal form is were.
If I were you, I would ask for help. It sounds formal, and the test asks for it.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Active: who did it comes first. Passive: what it was done to comes first.
Rabia broke the mug — active. The mug was broken by Rabia — passive. Same event, different order.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — who or what is first?
line: If the doer is first, it is active. If the thing done to is first, it is passive. That single question answers almost every active-or-passive question in the test.

section: step 2 — look for was or were plus a verb
line: was broken, are harmed, is maintained — that shape is passive. Passive almost always has a form of 'to be' in front of the verb.
The treasure was stolen — passive, and nobody says who did it. That is why the passive gets used: it lets you leave the doer out.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Standard English is the form used in writing and in formal speaking. It is not better English — it is the expected one.
We was going. We were going. Both are said out loud every day, but only one is Standard.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — was is for one, were is for more
line: I was, he was. We were, they were. This one rule covers most of the marks in this part of the test.
done needs a helper: I have done. On its own it is did. Same for seen and saw, been and was. The helper is the deciding thing.

section: step 3 — could have, never could of
line: It sounds like 'of' when spoken quickly. It is never written that way. It is have, shortened to 've. That is why it sounds like of.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Formal writing is what you use for a letter to a head teacher. Informal is what you use to a friend.
ask becomes request. buy becomes purchase. Same meaning, different clothes.
Here is how to do it.
A stranger in a position of authority gets the formal word. Formality is about the reader, not about the writer being clever.

section: step 2 — formal words are often longer
line: think about becomes consider. find out becomes discover. Two-word verbs are usually the informal one. One long word is usually the formal one.
Formal does not mean strange. It still has to sound like English. The test offers one word that is too odd on purpose. Leave it.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.

The spoken words go inside the inverted commas.
Here is how to do it.
Where are you going Only these go inside.
Open and close the inverted commas round them. Like a speech bubble.

Two jobs, one mark. An apostrophe either shows that something belongs to someone, or that letters are missing.
The dog's bowl is one dog. The dogs' bowl is more than one dog. That single mark changes how many dogs there are.
Here is how to do it.
Work out the owner first, before you write anything. The apostrophe goes straight after the owner, and the owner is not always what you expect.
One car, so the apostrophe goes before the s: the car's horn. You are not making it plural. You are saying it belongs to one thing.
Several teachers, so the apostrophe goes after the s: the teachers' room. Say the owner out loud first. If it already ends in s, the apostrophe goes after it.
An apostrophe also shows where letters are missing. The apostrophe goes where the letters were.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.

A list of what to bring, set out as bullet points.
The test checks the points are set out the same way.
Here is how to do it.
An introducing sentence, then a colon. It says a list is coming.

section: step 2 — • a cup / • a tea bag
line: Every point starts the same way. All lower case, or all capitals.
Same punctuation at the end of each point. Consistency is what gets the mark.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Synonyms are words that mean nearly the same. Nearly, not exactly — that is why they are useful.
This is the most-asked thing in the whole English test. Eight times in three years.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — put it in the sentence
line: Swap the word in and see whether the sentence still means the same. A synonym has to fit the sentence, not just the dictionary.
vast is bigger than big. furious is angrier than annoyed. The test often offers a word with the right meaning but the wrong strength.
One will fit better than the rest. Choosing the first one that looks right is how these marks get lost.
An antonym means the opposite. Check whether the question asks for the same or the opposite.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A prefix goes on the front of a word and changes its meaning. Usually to the opposite.
im, in, dis, un, de, mis, re, over. Which one depends on the word, and you mostly know by ear.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — say it with each one
line: unpossible sounds wrong. impossible sounds right. Your ear has heard these thousands of times. It is more reliable than a rule here.

section: step 2 — im before m and p
line: impossible, immature, impatient. This one is an actual rule and it holds almost always.
imposible is a spelling mistake, not a prefix mistake. The prefix joins on. Nothing gets removed from the word underneath.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A suffix goes on the end. It usually changes what job the word does.
develop is a verb. development is a noun. Same word, different job.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — what job do you need?
line: -ment and -ness make nouns. -ous and -ful make adjectives. -ly makes adverbs. Knowing what job you need narrows the choice to one or two straight away.
outrage becomes outrageous. beauty becomes beautiful. y usually turns into i, and a silent e often drops. Those two cover most of it.

section: step 3 — check it against a sentence
line: 'the development of the town' works. 'the developness' does not. If you cannot say it in a sentence, it is not the right suffix.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
You hear a word, and a sentence with a gap. You write the word in.
Twenty words, twenty marks. Each one belongs to a spelling pattern, and the patterns come back every year.
Here is how to do it.
Say the word slowly and listen for the pattern at the end. Most spelling marks are lost by writing what a word sounds like. The pattern tells you more than the sound.
Four spellings, one sound. Which one you need depends on the word it came from. solve becomes solution, permit becomes permission. Find the word underneath.

section: step 3 — write it, then read it back
line: Check it looks right, not just sounds right. You have seen these words in books hundreds of times. Trust your eye.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.

The market was bustling.
You may not know a word, but the words around it are clues.
Here is how to do it.
Traders calling, children running, a radio playing. The sentence gives the meaning away.
Put your guess in place of the word. If it still makes sense, you’re right.
bustling means full of busy activity. Check it fits the rest of the paragraph.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
How many years had Grandfather made the crossing?
Retrieval means finding the answer in the text, not making it up.
Here is how to do it.
Look for ‘years’ or ‘crossing’. Skim the text for it.
“every winter for forty years” The answer is near the key word.
forty If it says copy, copy the exact words.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Which title best sums up paragraphs 4 to 6?
Summarising means the main idea, not one small detail.
Here is how to do it.
Ama starts scared and ends brave. Look at the beginning and the end.
The engine and the glasses are just details. A summary covers the whole part.
It sums up the change. Check it fits every paragraph.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Ama says “No” a little too quickly.
The writer doesn’t say she’s scared. You work it out.
Here is how to do it.

section: step 1 — what does she do or say?
line: She answers too fast. Actions and words are clues.
She’s hiding her fear. That’s the inference.
“a little too quickly” Always back it up with words from the text.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Dark clouds pile up. The goats huddle under a tree.
The text doesn’t say it will rain, but the clues do.
Here is how to do it.
clouds, huddling goats, washing brought in Look at what is happening and how people act.
Rain. Use what you know about the world.
Because the clouds are dark and… A prediction needs a reason from the text.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Why are the steps in the recipe numbered?
Structure is how a text is organised, and why.
Here is how to do it.
Numbers, headings, paragraphs, a mirrored ending. Ask why the writer set it out that way.
Numbers tell you what to do first. Structure helps the reader.
It shows the order you must follow. Name the feature and its purpose.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
“an engine thudded like a slow heartbeat”
Writers choose words for their effect on you.
Here is how to do it.
like… : a simile. Simile, metaphor, personification, alliteration.
The engine to a heartbeat. Think of what a heartbeat is like.
The ship feels alive and calm. Say what it makes the reader think or feel.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
How are Ama and her grandfather different?
Comparing means finding what is alike and what is different.
Here is how to do it.
Ama grips the rail and steps back. Find evidence for each.
He rests his hands and laughs. Same kind of moment, different reaction.
She is nervous; he is calm. Use a word like whereas or but.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
